title: Line-level page meshing in the memory controller
idea: Imposed limit: no physical page may be less than 90% occupied. The controller keeps a 64 B-line indirection table, so two half-empty pages whose live lines do not overlap merge into one physical page without any change to virtual addresses; this brings Mesh-style compaction to unmanaged C/C++ heaps.
why: Fragmentation wastes 15-30% of heap memory in long-running services; meshing in hardware recovers most of it transparently.

title: Rover-hot DRAM: self-expiring banks for data that dies fast
idea: From rover electronics that run hot on tight power: let DRAM run at 95-105 C where retention falls to a few milliseconds, and allocate short-lived data (activations, streaming KV, packet buffers) into refresh-disabled self-expiring banks whose lifetime contract the compiler guarantees; only long-lived state sits in a small refreshed bank.
why: Hot-running memory enables dry cooling (on-site water >10x lower) while removing refresh energy (fact 3) for most bytes.

title: Piezoacoustic recirculating delay loops stream decode weights, skipping DRAM
idea: LLM decode reads every weight in the same fixed order each token, so a bank of GHz LiNbO3 bulk-acoustic delay loops on the interposer holds weight shards as circulating phonon pulses. The pulses are re-amplified each lap and timed to arrive exactly when the systolic array needs them. Piezo transducers convert bits to acoustic packets at ~10 Gb/s per loop, and thousands of loops form a sequential 'weight carousel'.
why: Takes deterministic weight streams out of DRAM: no row activations and no overfetch (facts 5, 8). Target is 20-40% less DRAM for small-batch inference, but each loop holds only ~10-100 kb, so it suits on-package buffers.

title: Fiber-optic Z-channel codes stretch unrefreshed retention to minutes
idea: Borrowed from asymmetric-channel coding in optical links: since leakage only flips charged cells to discharged (a Z-channel), data are inverted/encoded so ~90% of cells rest in the non-leaking state and protected with cheap unidirectional-error-correcting (Berger/Bose-Lin) codes; with the weak-cell tail corrected, the safe unrefreshed window grows from 64 ms toward minutes, long enough for natural rewrites or discard to cover all data.
why: Makes refresh-off operation practical for most data classes (zero refresh power) and lowers per-bit write energy by keeping most cells uncharged.

title: Endurance-budget tiering: unlimited endurance only where writes demand it
idea: From first principles, DRAM's unlimited endurance matters only for frequently written pages, and most resident bytes are written less than once an hour. Per-page write-rate counters in the controller migrate write-cold pages to a cheaper byte-addressable tier with limited endurance (NOR-like or high-bandwidth flash), and the controller enforces wear budgets.
why: If 50-70% of resident bytes are write-cold, DRAM per server can roughly halve while reads stay byte-addressable.

title: Hong Kong high-rises: 8-high hybrid-bonded SRAM as sole memory
idea: Borrowed from dense cities that build upward when land is scarce: eight thinned, capacitor-free SRAM dies on a mature node are hybrid-bonded onto an edge inference SoC for 0.5-1 GB of sub-5 ns on-package SRAM, and 2-bit weights let small models and their KV fit entirely, removing DRAM from the bill of materials.
why: Zero refresh and zero DRAM purchase for edge devices; stacking mature-node SRAM avoids EUV and the HBM TSV yield tax.

title: UNIVAC delay lines reborn: fiber loops as packet buffers
idea: From 1950s mercury delay-line memory: switch and NIC packet buffers are replaced by recirculating DWDM fiber loops where data is stored as light in flight and regenerated each lap by a semiconductor optical amplifier, with an SRAM index recording which time slot holds which packet.
why: Buffer DRAM/SRAM holds data that is only waiting; a 20 km loop at 1.6 Tb/s holds ~20 MB with no capacitor and no refresh.

title: Haiku poet's compression: distill long system prompts into gist tokens
idea: A haiku holds a scene in 17 syllables. A deployment's fixed 2-10k-token system prompt or tool manifest is distilled into 16-64 learned soft 'gist' tokens. Only those embeddings are trained, to match the model's outputs under the full prompt. The GPU cost is hundreds of dollars per deployment.
why: Agentic apps carry huge fixed prompts on every request. Gisting cuts per-request prefix KV and prefill by ~100x.

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game and VR memory. Neural textures give 4-8x over BCn, letting consoles, PCs and headsets ship with less DRAM.

title: Bell Labs ADPCM codec compresses KV cache along token axis
idea: Put a G.726-style adaptive differential PCM codec in the HBM base die: each key/value channel is predicted from the previous two tokens by a 2-tap adaptive predictor and only a 3-bit residual with adaptive step size is stored, decoded by a tiny MAC in the read path. Full-precision 'key frames' every 64 tokens bound drift.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory; exploiting token-to-token correlation gives 4-5x KV shrink beyond plain per-value quantization, freeing HBM for batch.

title: Teen texter's abbreviations: superword tokenizer adapter shrinks KV per document
idea: Teens write 'brb' for 'be right back'. An open model's tokenizer gains ~50k frequent multi-word tokens, and only the new embedding rows plus a light LoRA are trained (~$200k of compute). The same text then needs 25-35% fewer tokens, so it needs 25-35% fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory and prefill scale linearly with token count, so a 30% token cut is 30% less KV at any context length, and it stacks with quantization.

title: Scalable-video bit-planes: shed least-significant planes under memory pressure
idea: Borrowed from scalable video coding, where enhancement layers are dropped on congestion: tensors are stored bit-plane-major (MSB plane first), so the memory manager frees LSB planes in place when pressure rises, degrading precision gracefully without re-encoding; reads fetch only the planes that remain.
why: Makes capacity an elastic knob: a server absorbs 1.5-2x demand spikes by dropping planes instead of over-provisioning for peak.

title: Replay paging: record once, then run forever with oracle prefetch
idea: Po: memory arrives from the future. Recurring batch jobs (ETL, training epochs, nightly simulations) record their exact page-access trace on the first run; later runs replay it as a deterministic prefetch/evict schedule from SSD or CXL-flash, so DRAM holds only the lookahead window.
why: Repetitive jobs can run with 20-30% of peak working set in DRAM at near-zero stall, freeing capacity for interactive work.

title: Convert U.S. packaging and label printing lines to memory-offload films
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a contract-manufacturing program uses the large U.S. base of flexo/gravure packaging, label and thin-film PV coating lines, which already run kilometers of film at 10-50 um registration, to make the offload films in this cell: holographic ROM, sensor masks, e-paper, RFID logbooks and waveguide harnesses.
why: The U.S. makes ~1-2% of DRAM but has a large roll-to-roll converting industry; offload films reduce DRAM demand with domestic capacity in months, not 3-5-year fabs.

title: Unikernel diet: specialized library-OS images for every service
idea: Po: the operating system is part of the app. Services built with a domestic hardened toolchain are linked into single-address-space unikernels holding only the OS components they call, dropping per-VM kernel, init, daemon and page-table overhead from ~150-300 MB to ~10-20 MB.
why: In dense microservice fleets guest-OS overhead is 20-40% of DRAM; unikernels reclaim most of it on U.S.-made servers.

title: Reclaim ECC lanes for data and guard tensors with checksums
idea: Inverts 'every word needs hardware ECC': a 28 nm CXL controller uses the ECC chips' lanes as extra data capacity for regions holding ML weights and KV. Those regions are protected instead by per-tensor checksums, with a re-fetch from a golden copy on mismatch.
why: DDR5 RDIMMs spend 20% of their chips on ECC; reclaiming them for tolerant data adds ~25% usable capacity from modules already made.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel broadcasting one copy to a hall
idea: Decode reads every weight once per step in a fixed order, so weights need sequential access, not random access. Circulate one copy of a model's weights in a multicore WDM glass-fiber loop (InP lasers, thin-film lithium-niobate modulators, erbium amplifiers, periodic optical regeneration), and let every accelerator tap the passing stream through a passive coupler instead of holding the weights in HBM.
why: One copy in flight serves hundreds of accelerators, so weight HBM per GPU falls toward zero (weights are ~50-70% of inference HBM). Honest cost: per bit-second the loop burns more power than refresh (~0.1 nW vs ~0.7 pW per bit), and a 70B FP8 model at 100 Tb/s needs ~1,100 km of fiber, so it only wins through massive fan-out.

title: Runtimes pay per-byte rent and shrink caches automatically
idea: Imposed limit: every resident byte pays rent each second. The OS publishes a live DRAM price per GB-second; language runtimes (JVM, CPython, V8) and app caches expose value-per-byte curves and shrink memo tables, JIT code caches and object pools until the marginal hit value falls below the rent.
why: Software caches grow to fill whatever memory exists; price-driven shrinking can recover 10-30% of host DRAM without hard limits.

title: Mass-balance reconciliation: repair flips by enforcing data's built-in invariants
idea: Chemical plants reconcile noisy flow meters against mass-balance constraints. Data that already carries invariants (monotone CSR row offsets, sorted index arrays, distributions that sum to 1, histograms with known totals, rotation matrices) is stored raw in 1%-BER cells. On load, a reconciliation unit finds entries that violate the invariant and resets them to the least-squares value consistent with their neighbors, so the data's own structure replaces ECC. Delta-compressing the monotone arrays saves 2-4x on top.
why: Graph and sparse-matrix index arrays are a huge share of analytics DRAM; they can be delta-compressed and moved to cheap cells with no ECC overhead.

title: Backup-appliance dedup at cache-line granularity inside CXL expanders
idea: Borrowed from backup-appliance deduplication: the CXL expander hashes each 64-B line on write, keeps the hash in spare ECC/metadata bits, and maps identical lines to one physical copy through a reference-counted translation table; writes to shared lines trigger copy-on-write inside the controller.
why: Page-level dedup misses intra-page duplication; line-level catches repeated structs, zeros and tenant-shared weights for 1.3-2x capacity on typical cloud memory.

title: Sub-page MMU mapping merges sparse pages into one frame
idea: IFR: zero fragmentation. Closest: the MMU gains a 256 B mesh granularity inside 4 KB pages so two half-empty pages whose live slots do not overlap share one physical frame; a hardware bitmap scanner finds mergeable pairs.
why: Fragmentation wastes 10-30% of heap DRAM in long-running servers (Redis, browsers, JVMs); most of it is reclaimed.

title: Internal exchange leases stranded server DRAM by the GB-minute
idea: Box: share × datacenter market × GB-minute × auction-triggered × CXL switch or RDMA delivery. Each server offers its idle DRAM on an internal exchange; jobs bid for GB-minutes delivered over the pooled fabric and owners' budgets are credited.
why: 25–40% of fleet DRAM sits idle at any moment; recapturing it cuts new DRAM purchases 10–25%.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.
why: Billion-vector RAG and search indexes shrink ~25x in DRAM at about a 1-point recall loss, with unchanged DDR.

title: Live-morphing data structures between dense and succinct forms
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: runtime libraries let every hash map, vector and index switch representation online, morphing cold instances into succinct forms (Elias-Fano, rank/select bitvectors, minimal perfect hashes) and expanding hot ones back to pointer-rich forms, driven by sampled access counts.
why: Much in-memory data is cold but must stay in DRAM; succinct forms are 3-10x smaller, giving 1.5-2.5x heap reduction in data-heavy services.

title: KV cache as inverted-file vector index with DRAM-resident centroids
idea: IFR: context length is free. Closest: KV blocks are clustered online into an IVF index stored in flash; DRAM holds only the centroids and a recent window, and each decode query fetches its top-k clusters for sparse attention.
why: DRAM per million-token context falls 20-50x with ~1% quality loss on retrieval-heavy tasks.

title: Sampling working-set monitor chip that shrink-wraps container limits
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells: a 180 nm chip on the module samples 1-in-1024 accesses into a count-min sketch per 2 MB region and reports true working sets, letting the OS shrink each container's memory 'shell' to fit and reclaim the remainder to compressed or far tiers.
why: Containers are over-provisioned 30-50%; accurate hardware working-set data supports 20-30% reclaim without performance cliffs.

title: IBM 360 card-capacitor ROM stacked as thin-film back-end layers
idea: Revive CCROS, the System/360 card-capacitor read-only store: each layer is a word-line metal, a thin dielectric and a bit-line metal, with a '1' wherever an e-beam-defined coupling pad exists, and pulsing a word line couples charge onto the bit lines with no transistor or diode in the array. Dozens of layers stack using only deposition and patterning.
why: A 3D frozen-weight ROM made entirely from back-end steps any university nanofab has; multi-level pad sizes give 2 bits per crossing, so weights cost a few patterning steps per layer instead of DRAM.

title: Minify serverless memory: fork thousands from one golden snapshot
idea: Minify per-instance memory: each function runtime is pre-initialized once (imports, JIT, models loaded) and every instance forks copy-on-write from that golden snapshot in microseconds, holding only its private dirty pages (~3-8%).
why: Serverless and agent sandboxes fit 10-30x more instances per GB.

title: One nested weight set serves every model size
idea: Imposed limit: a provider may store one weight set per model family. Transformers are trained matryoshka-nested, so each smaller model is a prefix (a subset of neurons, heads and layers) of the largest, and the 8B, 30B and 120B tiers are all served from one resident copy by masking.
why: Providers keep several model sizes resident; nesting removes the duplicates and cuts weight DRAM ~1.5-2x across a model family.

title: Swap fp16 attention keys for product-quantized codes scored by lookup
idea: Substitute arithmetic on dequantized keys with table lookups. Each cached key becomes 8-16 one-byte product-quantization codes; at decode the query builds a small sub-vector dot-product table, and scores are summed from lookups over the codes, while values use 2-4-bit group quantization. This runs on existing GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Shrinks the KV cache 6-10x and the bytes read per token similarly (fact 5), so the same HBM serves several times more context.

title: Swap full KV heads for a shared low-rank latent via SVD retrofit
idea: Substitute full K and V with one latent per token: an existing model's K and V projections are factored jointly by SVD into a rank-r down-projection, the up-projections are absorbed into the query and output matrices, and a brief fine-tune follows (an MLA-style retrofit). This runs on today's GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Cuts KV 4-8x for models already deployed, without pretraining from scratch.

title: Magnify bit-level ops: hardware rank/select for succinct structures
idea: Magnify ISA support for succinct data: single-cycle rank/select and wavelet-tree access instructions, plus a near-memory FM-index unit, make compressed bitvector tries, suffix arrays and indexes as fast as pointer-based ones.
why: Indexes, tries and genomic search structures shrink ~3-8x toward their information-theoretic minimum.

title: Compiler region inference sizes heaps to the exact peak live set
idea: IFR: programs allocate exactly what they use at each instant. The constraint pushes to zero new hardware: a whole-program region-inference compiler (lifetime analysis in the style of Rust/MLKit) assigns every allocation to a stack-like region freed in bulk, removing allocator slack, fragmentation and GC headroom.
why: Cuts footprint 25-50% for allocation-heavy services with zero materials of any kind.

title: Bonsai pruning: memory-side unit trims never-attended KV tokens
idea: Prune what never sees light: the accelerator streams per-token attention-mass sums to a small memory-side 'bonsai' unit that keeps exponentially decayed importance per KV block and evicts or downgrades blocks below threshold in the background, off the decode critical path.
why: Most long-context tokens get negligible attention; 3-8x KV reduction at small quality loss with zero decode stall.

title: Lithium niobate domain-wall cells store write-once KV caches
idea: Each KV entry is written once per token and read many times, so store it in thin-film LiNbO3 domain-wall memory. A voltage pulse creates a conductive head-to-head domain wall between electrodes, and reading the wall current is non-destructive. LiNbO3's 1140 C Curie point keeps walls pinned for 10 years at 125 C, and 1e8+ cycles is plenty for one write per session.
why: Nonvolatile, refresh-free KV for in-vehicle LLMs lets prefix caches persist across sessions, and KV leaves DRAM entirely.

title: Mesh merging: two half-empty heap pages share one frame
idea: Break the one-virtual-page-per-frame rule: a malloc runtime randomizes object placement so sparse pages rarely collide, finds page pairs whose live objects don't overlap, and remaps both virtual pages onto one physical frame.
why: Compacts fragmented C/C++ heaps 15-40% without moving pointers, in software on existing DRAM; no rare-gas fab steps for new bits.

title: Swap local phone LPDDR for pooled edge DRAM for background apps
idea: Substitute on-device RAM with a shared edge pool. Phones freeze background apps and stream their compressed process images to edge-cloud DRAM over 5G and Wi-Fi, then restore them lazily through page-fault streaming. Statistical multiplexing lets one edge GB serve many phones.
why: Phones are roughly a third of DRAM bits and carry 8-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm. Phones could ship with 30-50% less LPDDR, with a much smaller pooled amount at the edge.

title: Mine-tailings reprocessing: keep token IDs, recompute evicted KV on demand
idea: Mines reprocess old tailings when a new assay shows value. Evicted KV entries are discarded, but their 2-byte token IDs and a 16-bit key sketch (random-projection signs) are kept. When a new query's sketch dot product flags a tailings span as relevant, the KV for that span plus its neighbors is recomputed by a short prefill and spliced back.
why: For cold spans, KV memory goes from context x layers x dims down to about 4 bytes per token, a 100x+ cut for million-token contexts; the recompute cost is paid only when a span is relevant.

title: Kintsugi potter repairs cracks: reuse DIMMs with known-bad rows
idea: Kintsugi makes cracked pottery whole and valuable. A ~$50k automated tester maps the failing rows of scrapped or factory-reject DIMMs and writes the bad-row map into a small SPD/EEPROM sidecar. A Linux boot-time driver reads the map and permanently retires those pages, so each DIMM serves ~99.9% of its capacity.
why: Many field returns and test rejects fail in only a handful of rows. Reclaiming them adds usable supply at ~zero silicon cost and also cuts e-waste.

title: Accountant's shadow price: bill every team DRAM at 2026 spot
idea: An accountant makes hidden costs visible. A chargeback tool reads each service's resident GB-hours from cgroup stats and bills them at the current 4x contract price in dashboards, PR comments and quarterly budgets, with a savings leaderboard. The tool costs under $300k; the rest of the budget funds pilots at three companies.
why: Once memory is a visible line item, teams typically cut 15-30% within a year through heap caps, cache sizing and replica trimming. It is a policy lever with near-zero capital.

title: Swap HBM-resident KV for attention-computing commodity DDR PIM DIMMs
idea: Substitute expensive HBM bits with cheap DDR bits. The KV cache moves to DDR5 DIMMs whose buffer chips hold bank-group dot-product and softmax units; the GPU sends only the query vector and gets back the attention output, so KV bytes never cross the bus.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6). Moving KV, often more than half of HBM demand, to DDR PIM halves HBM per accelerator, needs ~3x less wafer per KV bit, and cuts data-movement pJ (fact 5).

title: Profile-guided compiler narrows over-wide fields with overflow traps
idea: Box: representation shrink × compiler × struct field × profile-guided × narrow + reorder + trap. Fields whose observed ranges fit fewer bits (int64 counters under 2^20, enums, flags) are narrowed and packed, with cheap overflow traps that re-widen via deoptimization.
why: Padding and over-wide fields waste 20–40% of in-memory object bytes.

title: Sleep-consolidation pass re-encoding memory during idle troughs
idea: This borrows from how sleep consolidates memory. In nightly or between-batch idle windows, a host daemon re-encodes cold resident data with slow, strong codecs that are too expensive online: zstd-19, learned dictionaries, global dedup and struct-of-arrays relayout. Online paths only ever decompress with cheap decoders.
why: Asymmetric codecs reach 3-4x where online-speed codecs get about 2x. Spending off-peak compute shrinks daytime DRAM for cold data by 30-50%.

title: Minify replica count: consolidate long-tail models by global routing
idea: Minify how many places each model's weights must be resident: a global router concentrates all traffic for each long-tail model onto the fewest replicas that meet the SLO, and cold models page in from NVMe in under a second.
why: Pinned weight DRAM for fleets of thousands of models falls >=10x, which turns DRAM spend into a scheduling problem.

title: Swap random request placement for document-affinity routing of long contexts
idea: Substitute random load balancing with context-aware routing. The balancer fingerprints each request's large shared context (a codebase, a contract, a transcript) and sends every request on that context to one GPU group, replicating hot documents only when queue depth demands.
why: The same document KV is otherwise duplicated across replicas. Affinity turns N copies into ~1-2, saving 3-10x KV for shared documents, with no hardware change.

title: 28 nm CXL controller with inline zero-line and base-delta compression
idea: Inverts 'compression costs host CPU cycles': a CXL expander ASIC built on existing 28 nm lines removes zero lines and applies base-delta-immediate compression per 64 B line, with a small metadata cache, and exposes about 2x the physical DRAM as logical capacity.
why: Hardware line compression yields 1.5-2.2x on server heaps and needs only trailing-node logic, not leading-edge DRAM.

title: Wire-bonded 16-high stacks of trailing-node DRAM, no TSVs
idea: Inverts 'dense memory needs TSV stacking': staircase wire-bonded stacks of 16 thinned dies from mature DRAM nodes, built on existing OSAT lines, form capacity-only packages for CXL modules, where GB per slot matters more than bandwidth per package.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV area and yield tax and delivers high GB per module from existing fabs and packaging lines.

title: Subsea capsule lesson: sealed seawater-cooled shared memory pools
idea: From sealed subsea datacenter capsules: rack-scale CXL memory pools shared by dozens of hosts are built as sealed nitrogen-filled pods cooled through a seawater heat exchanger, while pooling removes each host's peak-provisioning margin.
why: Uses zero freshwater for cooling (>10x cut versus evaporative towers), and pooling cuts total DRAM 20-35%.

title: Utility meters, not itemized bills: fixed-size recurrent state in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from utility meters that keep a running total instead of every transaction: most attention layers are replaced by fixed-size recurrent/state-space states (a few MB per sequence) held in SRAM, plus a few exact-attention layers over a short local window.
why: Removes the linearly growing KV cache from DRAM; per-sequence memory becomes constant and fits on-die, so refresh power is zero.

title: Hybrid state-space retrofit replaces most attention layers' KV
idea: IFR: context costs constant memory. Closest with no new hardware: replace 7 of every 8 attention layers in a trained model with linear-recurrent state-space layers (fixed-size state) distilled from the originals, keeping one attention layer in eight for exact recall.
why: ~8x KV reduction for long contexts at modest quality cost.

title: Feature-phone NOR XIP, fixed: profile-clustered execute-in-place, DRAM-less SoCs
idea: Execute-in-place from NOR flash ran feature phones with little DRAM but was abandoned as code bloated and random fetches stalled. Profile-guided linking clusters hot code and read-only data into contiguous flash pages fronted by a 32-64 MB on-die SRAM cache, so edge AI devices, IoT and controllers ship with zero DRAM.
why: Removes DRAM entirely from billions of low-end devices, freeing supply for servers.

title: Rumor memory: erasure-coded replicas instead of triple copies
idea: Po: data exists only as rumors spread among neighbors. In-memory databases and caches replace 3x replication with Reed-Solomon (e.g., 8+3) striping across nodes' DRAM and rebuild lost shards over RDMA on failure.
why: Cuts DRAM spent on fault tolerance from 200% overhead to ~37%, freeing about half of total memory in replicated stores.

title: Racing the beam: framebuffer-free composition at scanout
idea: From the Atari 2600, which had 128 bytes of RAM and drew each scanline just in time: display controllers composite UI layers, video planes and overlays line by line from tile lists at scanout, keeping a few line buffers in SRAM instead of triple-buffered 4K/8K framebuffers and intermediate surfaces in DRAM.
why: Phones, cars and PCs hold 100-500 MB of framebuffers and surfaces; line-buffer composition removes most of it plus its DRAM bandwidth (fact 5).

title: Eliminate stored weights: regenerate weight blocks from PRNG seeds
idea: Each weight block is replaced by a seed plus 4-8 coefficients that combine LFSR-generated pseudo-random basis vectors; banks of on-chip LFSRs regenerate the block at use time, so DRAM holds only seeds and coefficients.
why: 3-5x weight compression with no DRAM bandwidth for the regenerated part; attacks capacity and data-movement energy.

title: G-code memory: store the toolpath, regenerate the part
idea: A 3D printer stores G-code, not the finished object. In the same way, deterministic data (positional-encoding tables, attention and dropout masks, index arrays, hashed embeddings, PRNG-initialized weights, procedural textures) is replaced by a 'toolpath' descriptor: kernel ID, seed and parameters. A tiny micro-sequencer on the CXL or DIMM buffer regenerates any line on load, and a page-table bit marks procedural pages.
why: Removes the 5-20% of AI and graphics footprint that is regenerable data stored for no reason; regenerating a line costs a few ns instead of DRAM bits.

title: Child says share your toys: one host copy of weights
idea: A child asks why ten pods load the same model ten times. An open-source daemon pins each model file once per host in hugepage-backed shared memory, and patched vLLM, TGI and PyTorch loaders mmap it read-only instead of keeping private host-RAM copies for staging, CPU offload and fast restart. Two engineers, ~9 months, ~$400k.
why: Inference hosts hold 4-8 duplicate host-RAM copies of the same weights. Dedup frees hundreds of GB per node, so cheaper host SKUs can be bought.

title: STARAN associative processor as near-memory KV pre-filter
idea: Revive the Goodyear STARAN associative array: a TCAM beside the HBM stack holds a 64-bit SimHash of each cached key, the query hash is broadcast, and match lines fire for keys within a Hamming threshold. Only those ~1-3% candidates are fetched at full precision while the rest of the KV sits compressed in a slower tier.
why: Attention reads the full KV every token; a parallel associative pre-filter cuts KV bandwidth 10-50x and lets 70-90% of KV live outside HBM.

title: Harvest laptop and console DRAM from e-waste into CXL sleds
idea: Reverse the supply chain: automated desolder, reball and burn-in lines pull DDR4/DDR5 BGA packages from recycled laptops, consoles and SO-DIMMs, bin them by speed and retention, and remount them on CXL far-memory cards behind a compression controller.
why: E-waste holds large amounts of DRAM that is already made; reclaiming it adds U.S.-processed memory supply with no neon litho or helium use.

title: Fleet DIMM gleaning: telemetry-guided physical rebalancing of installed memory
idea: Rearrange the DIMMs already installed across a fleet: per-server memory telemetry finds hosts whose peak use never exceeds half their DRAM, and technicians pull those modules during routine maintenance and install them in memory-starved hosts of the same generation.
why: Fleets often have 20-30% of DRAM never touched; moving it costs far less than buying new bits at 4x prices and needs no rare gases.

title: Fading KV: tokens lose bits as attention ignores them
idea: Po: memory that shrinks when you look away. Each KV entry carries an attention-usage counter and steps down 16 to 8 to 4 to 2 bits, then merges into a pooled summary vector, as its cumulative attention mass decays, mimicking human memory consolidation.
why: Most long-context tokens get negligible attention; graded decay gives 4-8x KV reduction with smoother quality loss than hard eviction.

title: Inference fleet single copy: optically multicast weights to many GPUs
idea: From the extreme of serving one giant model on thousands of GPUs: instead of replicating weights in every replica's HBM, a pooled weight memory streams each layer once per step over an optical multicast fabric to 32-64 accelerators that consume it in lockstep, so HBM holds only KV and activations.
why: Weight replication is often 10-60x across replicas; single-copy streaming cuts fleet HBM bits ~10x, and with them the most water-intensive bits the industry makes.

title: Newspaper memory: reprint embedding-table snapshot daily on microdot film
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): each night a maskless electrohydrodynamic-jet printer writes the recommender's long-tail embedding rows as ~2 um microdots on PET sheets, read by lenslet-coupled CMOS image sensors. By day DRAM holds only hot rows plus a delta log of updates since the print, and yesterday's sheet is recycled.
why: Long-tail embeddings are terabytes and rarely updated; a daily printed snapshot at under $1/GB, with DRAM only for hot rows and deltas, could cut embedding DRAM 5-10x if millisecond tail reads can be hidden by session prefetch.

title: Flight recorder: MRAM intent journal makes DRAM a crash-safe cache
idea: Like an aircraft black box logging only essential parameters, a small MRAM ring records memory-tier metadata (page-map updates, dirty-line intents, epoch markers) so a flash-backed memory can treat DRAM purely as a volatile cache and rebuild consistent state after power loss.
why: Lets cheap NAND carry capacity with DRAM shrunk to the working set and no NVDIMM batteries; MRAM needed is ~0.1% of capacity.

title: Fiber delay-line loop memory for strictly periodic weight streams
idea: This revives delay-line memory at datacenter scale. Weights that are read in the same order every decode step circulate in a 40 km dense-WDM fiber spool (100 wavelengths x 400 Gb/s gives about 1 GB in flight on a ~200 us loop), kept alive by optical amplifiers. Accelerators tap the stream as it passes, because sequential lockstep access never needs random addressing.
why: It replaces DRAM capacity for repeatedly streamed read-only data with roughly $5k of fiber: GB-scale capacity with no DRAM wafers.

title: Minify copies: single-copy OS across NIC, kernel, app
idea: Minify the 2-4 duplicate copies of file and network data (NIC ring, page cache, user buffer, DB buffer pool) with an OS where one capability-guarded buffer is shared read-only by every layer. Double caching between the OS page cache and the database is banned.
why: I/O-heavy servers recover ~1.2-2x of DRAM now lost to redundant copies.

title: Osmium density: KV entropy-coded against in-block predictions
idea: Osmium is the densest element; each KV block is stored as an rANS-coded residual where each key is predicted from the previous token's key in the same block and each value from a learned linear map of its own key, both available in streaming order, and a hardware rANS decoder in the memory controller expands the stream.
why: Sequence and K-to-V redundancy plus entropy coding push KV toward ~1.5-2 bits per element instead of 16, so ~8-10x fewer bits are fetched per token (about 10x lower energy per access) and KV capacity grows ~8x (energy, density).

title: Customs declaration: pages declare tolerated error for lossy compression
idea: Goods declare their contents at the border: add 2 tolerance bits to page-table entries (exact, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1 relative error) that runtimes set for activations, gradients and embeddings, letting the memory controller apply lossy codecs (mantissa truncation, block floating point) to tagged pages. OS and firmware only.
why: Approximation-tolerant data is 30-60% of AI memory; lossy encoding gives 2-4x on that share.

title: Swap uncompressed line storage for controller compression with ECC-hidden metadata
idea: Substitute raw line storage with compressed lines whose compression tag hides in unused ECC code-space encodings. The SoC controller compresses each 64 B line (zero, base-delta, frequent-pattern) and packs compressible pages 2:1, with no separate metadata lookups. Standard DDR5 RDIMMs, JEDEC commands and timings stay unchanged, and the OS sees elastic capacity with a balloon for overflow.
why: Server memory typically compresses 1.5-2x. Hiding metadata in ECC removes the metadata-cache penalty that held back earlier schemes, giving 30-60% more effective capacity on existing DIMMs.

title: Compression pays for ECC: eight-chip DIMMs keep full protection
idea: Reverse 'ECC needs spare chips': the controller compresses each 64 B line by at least 8 bytes (most lines allow it) and writes the ECC into the freed space; the rare incompressible line goes to a small overflow region marked by a pointer flag.
why: Removes the two extra chips in each 10-chip DDR5 RDIMM rank: ~20% fewer DRAM bits bought for server-class reliability.

title: Exponent-dictionary storage for BF16 and FP8 tensors
idea: Measured from the data, the 8-bit exponent field of trained BF16 weights and activations holds only ~2.5-3 bits of entropy because values cluster within a few octaves. Logic on the HBM/CXL base die stores each 128-value block as 3-bit codes into a per-block 8-entry exponent palette plus raw sign and mantissa, with a raw fallback for outlier blocks.
why: Lossless ~1.4x smaller tensors (16 bits to ~11.4 bits per value) with bit-exact results, so a model that needed 8 HBM stacks fits in 6.

title: HBM base die Huffman-codes BF16 exponent planes on write
idea: Box: lossless entropy coding × HBM logic base die × 4 KB tensor tile × on write × static Huffman on the exponent plane. The base die splits BF16 words into raw sign/mantissa planes and an exponent plane coded at ~2.6 bits instead of 8, re-expanding on read, so the stack transparently holds and moves fewer bits.
why: Weights and KV dominate HBM and their exponents carry little entropy; ~1.4× capacity and TSV bandwidth per stack, softening the HBM wafer-area tax (fact 6) and data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: ANS entropy decoder in the HBM base die
idea: Worsen: store bf16 weights raw even though their exponents carry under 3 bits of entropy. Flip: store weights entropy-coded with rANS in HBM and decode them at line rate in logic on the HBM base die, so the GPU sees plain bf16 while the stack holds about 70% of the bytes.
why: Capacity and bandwidth: about 1.4x more model per stack losslessly; also about 30% fewer bits moved over the TSVs.

title: HBM base die evicts KV tokens by accumulated attention
idea: This adds zero DRAM masks; the change lives in the HBM4 custom logic base die. The base die snoops attention-score writes, keeps each token's accumulated attention in SRAM, and on its own demotes low-scoring tokens' KV to a compressed far tier while pinning attention-sink tokens. The memory itself decides what to forget, on a microsecond timescale.
why: KV footprint is 3-8x smaller at matched accuracy, and the GPU spends no cycles on eviction policy.

title: Learned indexes replace B-trees and hash directories
idea: Worsen: keep giant B-tree and hash-table indexes in DRAM. Flip: replace them with small learned models (piecewise-linear or recursive model indexes) that predict a key's position with a bounded error window searched on flash.
why: Cost: indexes shrink 100-1000x, so the DRAM bill for indexing large datasets falls by over 100x; trades rebuilds on distribution shift.

title: Swap ECC-chip overhead for end-to-end checksums on reloadable data
idea: Substitute hardware ECC with software integrity for data that can be reloaded. Model weights, container images and page-cache copies of files sit on non-ECC DIMMs, guarded by per-block hashes that a background scrubber checks; a mismatched block is simply re-read from SSD. ECC DIMMs keep only mutable state.
why: DDR5 ECC RDIMMs spend 20% of their chips (8 of 40 bits per subchannel) on ECC, and this reclaims those bits for the reloadable data class. Standard DIMMs and interfaces throughout.

title: Eliminate the decompressed copy: load units decode compressed formats natively
idea: CPU/GPU load-store units gain decoders for dictionary, delta and bit-packed columnar encodings, expanding values into registers, so DRAM only ever holds the compressed form and no decompressed working copy exists.
why: Analytics and columnar workloads get 2-4x effective DRAM capacity and proportionally less data-movement energy.

title: Generated embeddings: replace terabyte tables with tiny hash-fed networks
idea: Po: the table is stored inside a brain. Recommender embedding tables are replaced by a multi-hash encoder feeding a small MLP that generates each ID's embedding on the fly, with only the hottest ~1% of IDs cached explicitly.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale DRAM hogs in recommendation; generation cuts them 10-100x at modest compute cost.

title: Smart-window electrochromic glass as analog weight-stationary crossbars
idea: Ion intercalation in WO3/NiO films, the chemistry of US-made smart windows, holds a non-volatile analog conductance that changes only when ions are driven. Pattern crossbars of these cells on window-glass coating lines, so frozen inference weights sit in place as conductances and matrix-vector products happen through Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, with no weight bits in DRAM.
why: Frozen weights (~50-70% of inference memory) leave DRAM entirely, at ~fJ per MAC instead of pJ per fetched bit; coating lines in the US help manufacturability. Risks: slow ionic programming and drift.

title: Sleep consolidation: idle gaps distil sessions into persistent memory tokens
idea: Like the hippocampus replaying the day into cortex during sleep, while a chat or agent session is idle the server compresses its KV cache into ~64 learned memory tokens written to persistent flash and frees the DRAM; the session resumes by loading those tokens.
why: Idle sessions hold 60-90% of KV memory in chat serving; compact persistent summaries free most of it and survive power loss.

title: Calcium bone remodeling: collections reshape themselves to their observed load
idea: Bone remodels to the loads it carries (Wolff's law); the runtime watches each large collection's access mix and swaps a read-mostly boxed HashMap (~48 B/entry) for an open-addressing primitive array (~12 B/entry) or a sorted static array, switching back when write bursts appear.
why: Boxed collections in Java/Python/JS hold 3-5x more bytes than their data; automatic remodeling saves ~30-50% heap on cache-heavy services (density).

title: SmartNIC fuses page compression with far-memory transport
idea: Combine a 28 nm FPGA SmartNIC's packet pipeline with a page compressor: pages evicted to remote memory are compressed, encrypted and RDMA-sent in one pass, and on fault the NIC decompresses directly into the host page, so far memory costs no CPU and stores 2-3x more per remote GB.
why: Makes rack-level far memory over commodity Ethernet practical, so each server needs less local DRAM.

title: Everspin MRAM, fixed: MRAM write-combining journal makes NAND workable memory
idea: Everspin MRAM never reached Gb density, so it never replaced DRAM. Use a small MRAM as a nonvolatile write-combining journal in front of NAND: random 64 B stores land in MRAM at ns latency, are coalesced into full NAND pages in the background, and reads check the MRAM index first.
why: Lets NAND serve as main memory for write-active data, not just read-only data, with no DRAM buffer and no capacitor-backed power-loss protection.

title: Genotype embeddings regenerated in the memory controller
idea: Recommender embedding tables are TB-scale. Each ID is stored instead as an 8-16 byte genotype code, and a tiny shared decoder MLP in the CXL memory controller expands it into the full 128-512-dim phenotype vector in ~50 ns on read. The full table never exists in DRAM. This is a molecule-to-organism scale jump: store the recipe, not the body.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumer in ads/recsys fleets. This gives 10-50x fewer bytes at a small accuracy cost.

title: Algebraic views evaluated at the memory port
idea: Many resident tensors are cheap functions of others: GQA repeat_kv expansions, broadcasts, padding, transposes, rotary-embedded keys. Store only the base tensor plus a view descriptor, and have the load unit or a near-memory engine evaluate the view on each read. Work moves from write time to read time.
why: This removes expanded copies (up to 8x for GQA expansions) and padding, cutting activation and KV footprint by 10-40%.

title: Climate-model error contracts: malloc with a declared tolerance
idea: From climate and CFD codes that already accept lossy float compression: add malloc_lossy(size, abs_err) so the OS maps the region through a controller-side fixed-rate block-transform codec that guarantees the bound, with the bound recorded in the page table entry and checked by the codec on every write-back.
why: Float fields compress 4-10x inside physics-acceptable error; turns approximate memory into an enforceable contract and cuts DRAM for simulation and ML arrays 4-8x.

title: Staggered garbage-collection cycles sharing one pooled heap headroom
idea: Co-located JVM, Go and .NET processes each reserve 1.5-3x their live heap as headroom. A node-level coordinator staggers their GC cycles in time and lends a single shared headroom region (memfd plus ballooning) to whichever process is about to collect.
why: Headroom is multiplexed in time instead of replicated per process, for 20-40% less DRAM on managed-language fleets.

title: AlN resonator spectra read hundreds of ROM bits per wire
idea: Encode tokenizer, embedding and activation lookup tables as the mass-loading of AlN bulk-acoustic resonators, each tuned to a distinct frequency. One RF sweep on a shared line reads hundreds of resonators at once from their spectral peaks, so no row decoders are needed. A reference resonator cancels the ~-25 ppm/C temperature drift, and frozen mass-loads do not change at 125 C.
why: A dense, decoder-free ROM for static lookup data attacks periphery (fact 7) and moves MB-scale tables out of DRAM in edge devices.

title: One-metal passive bridge letting four accelerators share HBM stacks
idea: A silicon bridge with a single metal layer (one mask, no active devices) wires each HBM stack to two to four neighboring accelerator dies through an arbiter in the HBM base die. Capacity is statistically multiplexed at the package scale instead of hard-assigned per die.
why: Peak KV demand across dies is largely uncorrelated, so package HBM can be about 25-40% smaller for the same SLO, using a near-trivial interposer.

title: Felting: superpose many key-value pairs into one hypervector mat
idea: Felt mats thousands of fibers into one sheet with no single point of failure. Associative stores (retrieval caches, semantic caches, feature stores) bind each key and value into a 10k-bit hypervector and bundle hundreds of pairs into one stored vector by majority sum. A lookup unbinds with the key and cleans up against a small codebook, and the representation survives even 10% bit flips.
why: Holds hundreds of approximate associations per 1.25 KB vector, 5-20x denser than hash tables for approximate-lookup workloads, and natively immune to 1% BER.

title: Typing-indicator KV prefetch for hibernated chat sessions
idea: When a response finishes, the server spills that session's KV cache to NVMe/CXL flash. It prefetches the cache back into HBM when the client sends a 'user started typing' or 'tab focused' event. This jumps from the nanosecond scale of HBM to the 5-60 s of human think time between turns, which hides a 10-200 ms restore completely.
why: HBM capacity and data movement (fact 5): live chat sessions are idle more than 90% of wall-clock time, yet their KV dominates inference HBM. Keeping only the actively decoding sessions resident cuts resident KV bytes about 5-15x.

title: Random-telegraph-noise dither enables unbiased 2-bit KV caches
idea: Quantize KV values to 2 bits with stochastic rounding, which keeps the expectation unbiased. The random bits come from single-trap random telegraph noise in minimum-size transistors. Trap switching speeds up at 125 C, so the entropy source gets better with heat over the 10-year life.
why: 2-bit KV with near-4-bit accuracy cuts KV memory 8x versus FP16.

title: Charge-trap flash computes attention over cold tokens in place
idea: KV tokens older than a recency window are programmed by Fowler-Nordheim tunneling into charge-trap NAND strings as analog conductances. The query is applied as wordline voltages, and bitline currents sum the dot products, so the array returns only the attention-weighted value sum. DRAM keeps just the last few thousand tokens.
why: KV for 1M-token contexts lives in NAND bits that are ~10x cheaper, and the DRAM KV footprint drops 10-100x (facts 4, 5).

title: Printed resistive crossbar compresses e-skin signals before digitization
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): on a printed tactile skin with thousands of taxels, a co-printed resistor-ladder crossbar applies a fixed learned projection to the analog taxel signals by Kirchhoff current summing, so only a 32-64-value embedding per frame is digitized and buffered instead of every taxel.
why: Robot hands and smart-surface arrays buffer raw high-channel streams; analog projection at the source cuts buffer DRAM and ADC count 20-50x.

title: Frozen shared interpreter heaps mapped by every worker process
idea: Box: share × language runtime × immutable object arena × interpreter startup × mmap-shared snapshot. Python/Node/Ruby servers freeze imported modules, bytecode, constants and read-only model data into a snapshot arena mapped read-only by all workers, with immortal objects so refcount writes no longer un-share pages.
why: Multi-worker servers duplicate hundreds of MB per worker; sharing frozen arenas cuts their RSS 30–60% with a pure software change and no fluorinated inputs.

title: Bullwhip damping: cache each block in exactly one stack layer
idea: Like supply chains where every tier hoards safety stock, the app cache, runtime, OS page cache, hypervisor and storage controller each cache the same block; a cross-layer exclusive-caching protocol passes block ownership tokens on eviction so each block lives in exactly one layer.
why: Duplicate caching wastes 20-40% of server DRAM in database and AI data-loading stacks.

title: Game-cartridge model distribution: sealed ROM weight modules sold per version
idea: Copy the NES/Game Boy cartridge business: model vendors ship each release as a sealed, keyed module of wide-parallel mask-ROM dies that plugs into a standard high-bandwidth slot on inference servers. Upgrades are cartridge swaps, the weight license rides with the hardware, and retired cartridges flow to a secondary market for edge and enterprise boxes.
why: Moves static-weight storage, 40-70% of DRAM bought for inference fleets, out of the scarce DRAM market into mask-ROM made on depreciated fabs; also keeps plaintext weights out of DRAM.
